$comment: Stack-agnostic production guard patterns. Stack modules add their own via stacks/<name>/guard.json, which is merged on top of this. Patterns are Python regex, matched case-insensitively against the full command string after normalisation.

deny.reason: DROP against a database. Schema changes belong in a reviewed migration, never an ad-hoc command.

deny.$comment: Was the bare word, the same defect as sql-grant and found while fixing it. `s.truncate(80)`, `cat src/lib/truncate.ts` and a branch named for a spec about truncating titles were all blocked. The statement's shape is TRUNCATE, an optional TABLE/ONLY, exactly one object, then a terminator — one object, because that is what separates `TRUNCATE users;` from the English `truncate long titles`. End-of-line counts as a terminator so a heredoc statement without a semicolon is still caught; a comma counts because `TRUNCATE a, b;` is valid.
deny.reason: TRUNCATE deletes every row and is not recoverable from a trash can.
DELETE with no WHERE clause deletes every row.
deny.$comment: Terminator accepts a closing quote or paren so the rule still fires inside a command substitution.

deny.reason: UPDATE with no WHERE clause rewrites every row.

deny.$comment: Matched the bare words `grant` and `revoke`, which are ordinary English and ordinary product vocabulary. A spec called "Revoke an invite link" could not be started: `git checkout -b agent/SPEC-024-revoke-an-invite-link` was blocked, as were `cat src/lib/invites/revoke.ts` and listing the spec file. What distinguishes the SQL statement is its shape — a privilege named right after the verb and an object after ON, or role membership granted TO a role, or ALTER ROLE/USER. `canRevoke` and `revokedAt` never matched (no word boundary), but every standalone use of the word did.
deny.reason: Changing database privileges is a human-only operation.
Database connection string pointing somewhere that is not localhost.
Database connection string pointing somewhere that is not localhost.
Database connection string pointing somewhere that is not localhost.
Database client pointed at a remote host.
Force push discards history irreversibly. Use --force-with-lease if you truly mean it, and only with a human present.

deny.$comment: Flags may be interleaved in any order — `git reset -q --hard` is the same command as `git reset --hard`. An earlier version required the two tokens to be adjacent and let the -q form through, which destroyed real work.

The flag has to be reaching a command that acts on it. Bare `--no-verify` matched anywhere in the string, so `grep -n "no-verify" base.json` — reading this very rule — was blocked as an attempt to bypass the gates. Searching for the name of a thing is not doing it. The environment-variable forms stay unanchored: those are prefixes, so their position already means they are being set rather than mentioned.
deny.reason: Bypassing quality gates. If a gate is wrong, fix the gate.

deny.$comment: Confined to one command segment. It used to span newlines and separators, so an rm on one line matched a .claude/hooks path on another — a lint command in the same block read as tampering. stacks/ is included because that is where each module's guard.json lives: deleting stacks/supabase/guard.json removes seven rules standing between a run and a remote database, and it was neither guarded here, denied in the profile, nor covered by the tamper fingerprint.

deny.reason: Recursive delete of a root, home or working directory.
deny.$comment: -rf, -fr, -r -f and --recursive --force are the same command. Match the flags independently rather than enumerating their arrangements. The terminator must also accept a closing quote or paren: inside `$(rm -rf ~)` the path is followed by `)"`, not whitespace.

Deliberately spans pipes and separators — `base64 -d <<< ... | psql` is the exact shape this exists to catch. Errs toward blocking; a false positive costs one human-run command. But the payload half listed `drop`, `delete` and `truncate` as bare words, so `node -e "s.truncate(80)"` read as an obfuscated database operation. Those now need the statement shape, exactly as the sql-* rules do; an obfuscated DROP TABLE still matches, because it is still a DROP TABLE. `production` likewise had to stop matching inside a filename — it blocked editing guard-production.py through a python heredoc — so it now requires the word to stand alone rather than sit inside a hyphenated name.
deny.reason: A database or production operation assembled indirectly — decoded, evaluated, or built inside another interpreter. Run it plainly so it can be read, or not at all.

deny.$comment: A script written this turn and immediately executed bypasses per-command inspection entirely.
deny.reason: Executing a script file whose name suggests it targets production. The guard cannot inspect what is inside a file — a human must run this.

push-to-default-branch: Removed deliberately. A run now owns its whole loop -- branch, commit, push, open the pull
request, poll CI, fix what CI finds, merge -- and this rule blocked legitimate steps of that
workflow while firing constantly on unrelated text: test fixtures, scripts, and commit
messages that merely mentioned a push.
What protects the default branch now is the path rather than a prohibition. Work reaches it
through deliver-run.sh, which re-runs the gates, checks coverage, asks the risk classifier and
waits for CI. A rule matching the string rather than the act was buying almost nothing and
Force pushes and history rewrites remain blocked. Those are unrecoverable; a merge is not.

$notes: A denylist cannot be complete. It is the third line of defence, not the first.
The first is that production write credentials do not exist on this machine.
The second is that the production role has no write grants, enforced by the database itself.
If a pattern here fires on legitimate work, do not weaken it silently — record the exception in docs/decisions/.
